title: Sorrow Turned to Celebration
overview: On the day set for their destruction, the Jews of Persia defeat those who attack them, and Mordecai and Esther establish the yearly feast of Purim to remember it.

parts.label: The day is reversed (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: This is the very date Haman's decree had chosen for wiping out the Jews, but a second royal order now lets them defend themselves. Local officials side with the Jews mainly because Mordecai has become so powerful at court.

parts.label: Fighting in Susa (vv. 5-10)
parts.note: The text is blunt about the killing, including 500 men in the capital and Haman's ten sons, and says the Jews did as they pleased to their enemies. They were allowed to take their enemies' property but refused, which many read as a sign they wanted survival, not gain.

parts.label: Esther asks for more (vv. 11-15)
parts.note: Esther asks for a second day of fighting in Susa and for the bodies of Haman's sons to be publicly displayed on poles, a way of shaming defeated enemies. The story does not explain her reasons, and readers have long argued whether this was needed for safety or was revenge.

parts.label: Across the empire (vv. 16-19)
parts.note: Elsewhere the Jews kill 75,000 attackers in one day, and some scholars doubt the large numbers are meant as exact history. Because Susa fought a day longer, villages celebrated on the 14th and the capital on the 15th, a split still kept today.

parts.label: Mordecai sets up Purim (vv. 20-28)
parts.note: Mordecai calls for a yearly feast with shared meals, gifts of food to friends and gifts to the poor. It is named Purim after the 'pur,' the lot Haman cast to pick the day of destruction, so the name itself recalls the plan that failed.

parts.label: Esther confirms it (vv. 29-32)
parts.note: Esther adds her royal authority to make Purim official, and Jewish communities still keep it by reading Esther aloud. The mention of 'fasting and lamentation' is unclear; it may recall Esther's earlier fast or point to fasts kept alongside the feast.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the story presents the Jews' violence as approved by God or simply records what happened without judging it, especially Esther's request for a second day.
think: When a people survives an attempt to destroy them, what do you think is worth remembering, and what is hard to hold alongside the celebration?
